title: Should Schools Ban AI?
author: The Busch School of Business
summary: This piece, published on the Superhabit newsletter and authored by a Busch School of Business faculty member, argues that the standard debate over AI in education — how to stop students from cheating with it — asks the wrong question, and lays out the school's alternative policy built around student formation rather than surveillance. Rather than a single blanket rule, the school lets each professor choose one of three options per course (AI forbidden, permitted, or encouraged), recommending more restrictive settings for freshman and sophomore courses and more permissive ones as students advance toward the job market. The most distinctive design choice is what happens in courses where AI is encouraged: students must submit both their prompts and their full dialogue with the AI, turning the interaction itself into a visible, assessable record of the student's judgment rather than treating the AI-generated output as the thing to catch or clear. Where a professor forbids AI, the burden falls on the faculty member to redesign the assessment itself — oral exams, in-class writing, real-time argument defense — rather than relying on detection software, which the essay explicitly rejects as treating 'students as suspects to be managed rather than people to be formed.' The piece frames this as more than a pedagogical choice: it's presented as consistent with the school's explicit mission to form students in virtue, arguing that moral and practical excellence converge once the goal shifts from catching misuse to cultivating judgment.
points: The three-tier policy (AI forbidden, permitted, or encouraged, chosen per course by the professor closest to the material) avoids a one-size-fits-all rule, letting AI's role scale with students' developmental stage and course-specific goals.

Requiring students in AI-encouraged courses to submit their full prompts and dialogue with the AI converts the interaction itself into an assessable artifact of judgment, a specific, replicable mechanism other institutions debating AI policy could adopt directly.

The explicit rejection of AI-detection software — 'a policy built entirely on surveillance treats students as suspects to be managed rather than people to be formed' — reframes the standard cheating-prevention approach as a values choice, not just a technical one, tying assessment design directly to how the institution treats students.
quotes: Does AI augment or undermine education? Teachers fear that because a student can generate an essay using these tools in a few seconds, the essay is dead, the exam is dead, and the university may be next.
This spring, our faculty agreed on an AI use policy for students where, for each course, the professor may choose one option: AI forbidden, AI permitted, or AI encouraged.
Most schools are asking: how do we stop students from cheating with AI? We asked: how do we ensure that AI use serves rather than subverts their formation?
we're asking faculty to require that students submit both their prompts and their dialogue with AI so that the tool is used for learning rather than to avoid learning.

When a professor chooses to forbid AI tools in a course, it is that faculty member's responsibility to design assignments so AI use is practically impossible: such as using oral examinations, in-class writing, or defending an argument in real time.
The Busch School refuses to instrumentalize anyone, and a policy built entirely on surveillance treats students as suspects to be managed rather than people to be formed.
Our students learn to use them well, and better than their competitors, because we seek to form their souls alongside their skills.
